best_moment.what: Wrote 40 appeal letters properly on a Tuesday night MPS, and the man whose case could not be reopened turned up with kueh. Small, human, no big speech, and it stuck with me.

worst_moment.what: The director asked if the system is a joke and I said nothing. It was an awkward, vague moment with no real choice to make, and I did not know what the game wanted me to feel.

answer.held_back_by: Nothing really held me back. I just kept making the sensible, honest choice and the game kept rewarding it. The only brake was STAND slipping a bit, and it never really bit.
answer.ending_fair_why: I got PM and the pay formula line was a nice jab, so it matched how I played. But the 'declassified' card telling me one choice at 40 changed my ceiling felt a bit sudden, since I did not know that choice was the big one.
answer.chase_next: I would try the greedy route: take the conglomerate board seat that pays more than the PM, and see whether the file stays boring or blows up. Also curious what the ending is if I stay a civil servant and never go into politics.
answer.play_again_why: It was a long run and I played it on instinct and mostly won. I would come back another day for the corrupt route, but not right now in bed.

DARREN LIM · THE FINAL POSITION
Prime Minister

You made it. The formula pays you twice the entry-grade minister's salary, and the formula was published, so nobody can say they were not told.

RETIRED AS Prime Minister
AT AGE 59
LIFETIME EARNINGS $39.97M
INTEGRITY 100

DECLASSIFIED
YOUR CEILING: When you joined, your file put no ceiling on you inside the service. Most people's files do.
THE PARTY'S ESTIMATE: When you won your seat, the party made its own: Senior Minister of State. Nobody told you that either.
THE YEAR IT CHANGED: At 40, in The Officer You Nominated, you chose "Let her decide without hearing from you." It raised your ceiling to Prime Minister.

LEGACY: People you trained quote you in rooms you will never enter. Two of them say you are the reason they stayed.
